title: POC: scaling cartography and response-entropy kickoff - Magneta Commerce
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark plan spreadsheet and template by 2027-10-01
Customer to provide 2 weeks of traffic trace (anonymized) and sample prompts by 2027-10-06
Schedule in-person bench run window (2 days) week of 2027-10-18
SE to provide initial QPS/concurrency sims by 2027-10-04
action_items: Maya - export and sanitize 14-day ingress traces (due 2027-10-06)
Alex - send pricing options for hosted vs dedicated pilot (due 2027-10-02)
Ravi - share sample prompts and 50 representative request/response pairs (due 2027-10-06)
summary: Kickoff scoping for a 4-week POC focusing on shaping Magneta's inference traffic cartography and measuring response entropy. Key goals: define success criteria (tail latency < 300ms p95 for short responses, p99 < 1s for long), establish workload sizing (baseline QPS, burst envelope, concurrency targets), design benchmark scenarios for accuracy vs cost trade-offs, and align timelines for data handoff and bench runs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Navarro: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll run about an hour — agenda is scope and success criteria for the POC. 
[00:18] Tom Yuen: Yep, thanks Alex. We're primarily trying to quantify cost and risk of moving our product recommendations and chat assistant to an external inference provider.
[00:27] Priya Patel: Great, can you give us a quick traffic snapshot, Tom — baseline QPS, typical request size, expected spikes?
[00:34] Maya Chen: Sure — baseline QPS is about 6 QPS during business hours, but we have these episodic flash promotions where we see 180 to 220 QPS for a 5 to 10 minute window.
[00:46] Tom Yuen: Right, and average input tokens are small on the recs calls ~30-60 tokens, but the assistant flows produce big outputs often 400 to 800 tokens.
[00:58] Jonah Rees: So input/output token skew is high — small prompt, long response. That affects KV cache locality and memory for autoreg.
[01:08] Maya Chen: Also note we have many long-running sessions where the user context builds up, so per-user state means some requests re-use long KV caches.
[01:19] Priya Patel: Are those statefull sessions pinned to a single shard or are you stateless?
[01:23] Ravi Sinha: We're mostly stateless, but we persist conversational context server-side and pass the full context down each call — so token length varies a lot.
[01:33] Alex Navarro: Ok, that's useful. For the POC we typically ask for a 14-day ingress trace, anonymized, plus 50 representative prompt/response pairs. That lets us synthesize workload shapes: baseline QPS, peak envelope, and token-length histogram.
[01:49] Tom Yuen: We can do that — Maya will handle sanitization. Two questions: what are the usual success criteria Redwood expects? And how do you measure response entropy?
[02:02] Priya Patel: Success criteria we'll propose: functional correctness (no degradation vs your current model >95% on selected evals), latency SLAs — for Magneta we'd recommend p95 < 300ms for short rec requests, p99 < 1s for long assistant responses, and cost targets relative to your on-prem run (reduce per-token infra cost by 20%).
[02:22] Priya Patel: Response entropy we compute via a set of per-prompt cross-entropy and sampling-stability metrics — basically measure variation across N=8 inference runs and look at KL and token-level perplexity drift. For the POC we'll add a human-review subset too.
[02:40] Maya Chen: Human review is important. We need to be sure we don't regress on hallucination rates.
[02:45] Alex Navarro: Noted. We'll include hallucination heuristics, plus a small manual eval deck.
[02:51] Tom Yuen: On infra, we need to discuss dedicated vs hosted. We can't send PII out of the VPC, plus our compliance team demands KMS/HSM integration.
[03:02] Jonah Rees: Redwood Private supports a VPC private control plane with customer-managed KMS; for the POC we can run in a dedicated tenant or a private deployment depending on timeline.
[03:12] Ravi Sinha: Timeline is tight — we want a go/no-go decision in 4 weeks so we can budget next quarter.
[03:18] Alex Navarro: Then our plan: week 1 — get traces and prompts; week 2 — finalize bench scenarios and config (quantization candidates, batch sizes, warm pools); week 3 — run bench (two day window); week 4 — analyze and present results. Does that align?
[03:35] Maya Chen: Yes. For bench runs, we need to exercise burst windows with 1:1 mix of recs and chat for some runs and 80/20 rec/chat for others.
[03:44] Priya Patel: Good — we'll create three bench scenarios: (A) steady-state 6 QPS with normal token mix; (B) burst envelope 200 QPS for 10 minutes with realistic token lengths; (C) tail stress test ramp to 500 QPS for 2 minutes to validate autoscale/fallback.
[03:59] Tom Yuen: For (C) are you simulating cold starts? Our product sees cold model invocations during major events.
[04:05] Jonah Rees: We can configure pre-warm pools and vary cache hit rates. We'll simulate cold starts and a warmed baseline. Cold starts are more relevant for hosted ephemeral nodes.
[04:16] Maya Chen: Also, do you support partial response streaming for the assistant? We rely on streaming to reduce perceived latency.
[04:23] Priya Patel: Yes, streaming is supported. We'll include p50 streaming latency and time-to-first-token metrics.
[04:29] Ravi Sinha: On tokenization, our pipeline currently uses a custom tokenizer variant; will that impact per-token accounting?
[04:36] Priya Patel: We usually align tokenization to the model's tokenizer; we'll need a small sample to verify effective token counts. If there are mismatches we normalize by char-level conversions for cost comparisons.
[04:47] Alex Navarro: Security ask noted. We'll attach SOC2 + ISO docs and a quick runbook for KMS integration.
[04:54] Tom Yuen: Great. On benchmarks, can you show cost projections for quantized LLM variants? Our cost model needs both FP16 and 4-bit QAT estimates.
[05:03] Priya Patel: Absolutely — we'll include model variants: float16 baseline, 8-bit quant, and 4-bit int8-ish profiles. We'll show expected throughput per GPU type and cost per 1M tokens for each.
[05:14] Maya Chen: Are kernel-level optimizations part of the POC? We currently rely on vendor-supplied runtimes.
[05:20] Jonah Rees: Redwood's serving runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution. In the bench we can test with both sequence-capped runs and real-length distributions to show sensitivity.
[05:31] Tom Yuen: About session affinity — if we have per-user KV caches, do you recommend sticky routing so users hit the same node?
[05:39] Priya Patel: For high cache reuse, session affinity helps a lot for tail latency. We can model both designs: affinity vs stateless with KV externalization; affinity reduces cross-node KV miss but increases hot-spot risk. We'll include both in the bench.
[05:55] Maya Chen: What's your default batch sizing strategy? We have tight p95 targets.
[06:00] Priya Patel: Default is latency-aware continuous batching — small batches on tails, larger when throughput allows. For your p95 targets we'll recommend aggressive prefix caching and small target batch windows (10-20ms) to keep p95 low.
[06:12] Ravi Sinha: Any recommended concurrency ceilings per GPU for our model? We run a ~7B-ish model.
[06:18] Jonah Rees: For a 7B at fp16 expect single GPU concurrency ~10-16 for interactive latencies; with 4-bit quant you can push higher concurrency but watch for increased variance. We'll provide benchmark numbers for your exact model config.
[06:32] Tom Yuen: On observability — what telemetry do you need from us to calibrate the bench?
[06:37] Alex Navarro: We'll need token-level size histograms, request timestamps, any routing keys, and error logs. A sample of user sessions helps rebuild heavy-tail behaviors.
[06:47] Maya Chen: We'll also share SLO definitions our product uses and what constitutes an incident.
[06:52] Priya Patel: Good. For the POC acceptance gates: 1) Bench meets p95/p99 latency targets under scenario A&B, 2) quality regression <5% on evals, 3) cost within target band, 4) security integrations validated in a sandbox.
[07:09] Tom Yuen: If the bench fails one of those, do you provide remediation cycles?
[07:13] Alex Navarro: Yes — we offer one remediation pass to tune caching/batching/quantization, with follow-up benching. Additional cycles are part of a scoped engagement.
[07:23] Ravi Sinha: Any concerns about stateful conversation context and token growth for multi-turn? We saw token inflation over long sessions.
[07:30] Priya Patel: We'll instrument token-growth curves and suggest truncation/summary strategies plus session embeddings to replace raw tokens when appropriate. We'll validate impact on quality as part of the human review.
[07:44] Maya Chen: For the runs, can you provide an example bench config?
[07:49] Jonah Rees: We'll share a bench template (link: short/redwood/bench-magenta) — includes scenarios A/B/C, sequence length distributions, and ramp profiles.
[07:58] Tom Yuen: Good. A couple of negotiation points — we might try a hybrid: dedicated pool for chat, hosted for recommender. Does Redwood support mixed routing?
[08:08] Alex Navarro: Yes, smart routing is supported; rules can route by endpoint, model size, or SLO class. We'll propose a hybrid pilot if you want.
[08:17] Maya Chen: The compliance team will want audit logs and per-request provenance; is that in the console?
[08:23] Priya Patel: Yes, trace-level logs with token counts, model version, and routing path are captured; retention can be configured. We can provide a sample export during the POC.
[08:33] Ravi Sinha: Great, will you include cost sensitivity when varying batch sizes and num replicas? We need an ops-friendly knob.
[08:40] Priya Patel: We'll produce a cost vs latency curve for each bench scenario and show the dominant dimension: more replicas lower latency but increase fixed cost; batching shows per-token amortization benefits.
[08:52] Tom Yuen: One more question — what about fallback behavior if dedicated capacity is saturated during a flash sale?
[08:59] Jonah Rees: We can configure fallback to the hosted fleet with graceful degradation policies: lower-response max length, reduce sampling temperature, or route to a smaller model. We'll test these in the tail stress scenario.
[09:12] Alex Navarro: Ok before we wrap — who owns the POC project plan on your side?
[09:16] Tom Yuen: Maya will be the internal owner, Ravi will be primary ML contact for sample artifacts.
[09:22] Alex Navarro: Perfect. We'll follow up with the benchmark template and a short security packet.
[09:26] Maya Chen: Thanks. Expect the traces by next Tuesday.
[09:30] Alex Navarro: Great, thanks everyone. We'll send notes and the spreadsheet.
[09:34] [meeting ends]
questions: How do you compute response entropy and what human review thresholds do you use?
Can Redwood simulate cold starts and pre-warm behaviors?
What observability artifacts are available for compliance (audit logs, per-token traces)?
